analysis.one_liner: Set voluntary Senate campaign spending limits, banned PAC money and party soft money, and gave candidates free TV time.
analysis.headline: The bill died when a vote to cut off debate won only 54 of the 60 senators it needed, with 46 of 47 Democrats in favor and 45 of 53 Republicans against.
analysis.plain_summary: Sponsored by Republican John McCain with mostly Democratic support, the bill would have set voluntary spending limits for Senate races and rewarded candidates who complied with free TV time, discounted ad rates, and cheaper postage. It banned political action committees from federal elections, shut down national parties' unregulated "soft money," capped candidates' use of their own wealth at $250,000, and required 60% of contributions to come from in-state individuals. It also required disclosure of bundled contributions, banned personal use of campaign funds, and barred election-year taxpayer-funded mass mailings by members running for reelection.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would gain a system in which Senate candidates could compete without depending on PAC checks, party soft money, or huge out-of-state donations: complying candidates would get 30 minutes of free broadcast time, ad rates cut to half a station's lowest price, and reduced postage, funded partly by ending members' election-year franked mass mailings. Candidates of modest means would benefit from the $250,000 cap on spending personal or family wealth, and the 60% in-state contribution requirement would force candidates back to their own constituents. Bundled contributions would have to be disclosed, and ads would have to carry a candidate's own "I approved" statement.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates without big-money backers

how_it_helps.text: Candidates who accepted spending limits would be rewarded with 30 minutes of free broadcast time, a guarantee that no station could charge more than 50% of its lowest rate, and reduced postage, while members were barred from sending franked mass mailings in their own election years.

It banned political action committees from contributing to federal candidates; if a court struck that ban, PAC giving would fall back to individual-sized limits and no more than 20% of a candidate's spending limit.

National parties would be barred from raising or spending unregulated soft money, and state parties would have to use fully disclosed, limit-compliant money for any activity that could affect a federal election.

Candidates seeking the benefits could spend no more than $250,000 of their own and family wealth and had to raise at least 60% of contributions from individuals in their own state, and bundlers — including registered lobbyists — would have to disclose the bundles they delivered.

It banned personal use of campaign funds, required broadcast ads to carry the candidate's own approval statement, and gave the Federal Election Commission power to seek court injunctions and run random post-election audits.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees would lose their channel into federal elections. National parties would lose the soft-money system that let them raise unlimited checks from corporations, unions, and large donors. Broadcasters and cable operators would have to donate airtime, sell ads at half their lowest rate, keep candidate ads on schedule, and risk license action for denying access. Wealthy candidates who want to bankroll their own campaigns would be capped at $250,000, and lobbyists and professional fundraisers would face disclosure of the money they bundle.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs, big donors, parties, and broadcasters

drawbacks.text: The spending limits were voluntary, and the bill answered a big-spending opponent by raising the complying candidate's cap in steps — 20% if the opponent spent 110% of the limit, 50% at 150%, and 100% at 200% — so total spending in a race could climb far above the stated cap.
Once $10,000 in outside independent spending appeared, a complying candidate's limit rose dollar-for-dollar to match it, so unregulated outside money could push spending upward without limit.

Mandating free airtime and half-price rates on broadcasters was legally contested at the time; the bill's own drafters included severability and a direct appeal route to the Supreme Court, acknowledging that parts of it might be struck down after years of litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest parts — the PAC ban and the soft-money ban — went to the root of special-interest money in Senate races, and the free-airtime and discount package gave candidates a realistic way to reach voters without huge fundraising. But the design was leaky: because the caps were voluntary, rich self-funders and outside groups could force the limits upward step by step, and the broadcast mandates invited a drawn-out court fight. The bill would have produced a real but partial cleanup, not a hard cap on campaign money.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate debated the bill in June 1996, but a vote to cut off debate — which needed 60 senators — got only 54, so opponents' extended debate killed it and it never received an up-or-down vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill in September 1995 with 18 cosponsors — 15 Democrats and 3 Republicans, including Russell Feingold.

The Senate Rules Committee held six sets of hearings between February and May 1996 but never voted the bill out; on June 20, 1996 the full Senate unanimously discharged the committee and began floor consideration.
On June 25, 1996, the Senate failed 54-46 to cut off debate, short of the 60 votes needed: 46 of 47 Democrats voted to proceed, while only 8 of 53 Republicans did.
The bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up again, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 with no final vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing money system: PACs, national parties' soft-money operations, large donors, and broadcasters all kept the rules that favored them because the bill died without a final vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big donors, PACs, parties, and broadcasters

for.name: John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, brought it to the Senate floor in June 1996, and voted to cut off debate.

for.name: Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill at its introduction.

for.name: 46 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted to cut off debate and let the bill come to an up-or-down vote.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Publicly pressed for campaign finance reform, and congressional allies used the June 1996 Senate debate to force the issue to a vote before the election.

against.name: 45 of 53 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cutting off debate, denying the bill the 60 votes it needed to reach a final vote.

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill during the June 1996 floor debate and backed continued debate that killed it.

against.name: National Association of Broadcasters
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the free-airtime and mandated-discount provisions that would have cost stations revenue and programming control.

sides.party_line_note: On the decisive cloture vote the split was heavily partisan: 46 of 47 Democrats voted to proceed while only 8 of 53 Republicans did, so the 45 Republican no votes killed the bill.

industries.note: Stations would have had to give complying Senate candidates up to 30 minutes of free airtime, sell ads at no more than half their lowest rate, keep candidate ads on schedule rather than preempting them, and risk license revocation for denying access — including on cable systems. The industry's interest in full rates and programming control ran directly against the public benefit of cheap candidate access to the airwaves.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, labor, and trade)
industries.note: The bill barred PACs from contributing to federal candidates entirely, with a fallback that would cut PAC giving to individual-sized limits and 20% of a candidate's spending limit. PACs exist as a channel for organized money into campaigns, and that channel is exactly what the bill closed.

National parties would have been barred from raising or spending unregulated soft money, and state parties would have had to use fully disclosed, limit-compliant funds for any activity affecting federal elections. This ended the parties' ability to take unlimited checks from large donors for election activity.

Registered lobbyists who bundled contributions would have had the bundles reported and treated partly as their own contributions, exposing the delivery of bundled money to candidates. Their value to clients depends on quiet access, which the disclosure provision would have reduced.

Candidates seeking the benefits could spend no more than $250,000 of personal and family wealth on a Senate race, so millionaires could no longer simply buy competitiveness. The cap protected candidates without personal fortunes.
